title: Interpolating a series
objectives: Write a linear interpolator that handles gaps, edges and unsorted input.

screens.title: Two gaps in a price
screens.prose: About two minutes a question; say your reasoning aloud first. A price reads 100, then two days are missing, then 112. Fill the gaps with equal steps.
screens.question: What goes in the first gap?

hints.text: Count the equal steps from 100 up to 112.
Two gaps and the landing on 112 make three steps.
$12 / 3 = 4$, so the gaps read 104 and 108.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count every step from 100 to 112, including the last.

byKey.half: You split the rise over two steps. There are three, because the last one lands on 112.
byKey.carry: You carried 100 forward. That ignores the 112 waiting on the other side.

explain.text: Three steps of 4 take 100 to 104, 108 and 112. This straight-line fill is linear interpolation.

screens.title: The formula on two points
screens.prose: Two known points, $(0, 100)$ and $(10, 200)$. A third sits at $x = 2.5$, on the straight line between them.
screens.question: What is $y$ at $x = 2.5$?

hints.text: How far across the gap is 2.5?
A quarter of the way. Which point is on the left? If points arrive in any order, sort by $x$ first.

feedback.correct: 125: a quarter of the way up a rise of 100.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the fraction of the gap, then add that fraction of the rise to 100.

byKey.rise: You found the quarter of the rise but forgot to add it to 100.
byKey.unit: You added 2.5 to 100, as if $y$ rose one for each unit of $x$. Here it rises ten.

explain.text: The point is $2.5/10 = 0.25$ of the way across. It gets 0.25 of the rise of 100 on top of the starting 100.

screens.title: Points in any order
screens.prose: The same task, but the points arrive unsorted: $(3, 30)$, $(1, 10)$, $(2, 25)$. Find $y$ at $x = 2.5$.
screens.question: What is $y$ at $x = 2.5$?

hints.text: Which two points sit either side of 2.5?
$x = 2$ and $x = 3$, which are the first and third rows listed.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Sort by $x$ and use the two points either side of 2.5.

byKey.listed: You used the first two listed points, $(3, 30)$ and $(1, 10)$. Sort by $x$ first.

explain.text: Sorted, the points either side of 2.5 are $(2, 25)$ and $(3, 30)$. Halfway between them is 27.5.

screens.title: Beyond the ends
screens.prose: Same points. Now ask at $x = 5$, past the largest $x$ of 3. The rule is to hold the nearest value.
screens.question: What is $y$ at $x = 5$?

hints.text: Is there a point on the far side of 5?
No. Hold the end value, the $y$ at the largest $x$.
The largest $x$ is 3, where $y$ is 30.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Past the last point, hold the last value.

byKey.extend: You extended the last segment, $(2, 25)$ to $(3, 30)$, past its end. That is extrapolation, not interpolation.

explain.text: Nothing brackets $x = 5$, so we return the nearest end value. At $x = 0$ the same rule returns 10.

screens.title: The same x twice
screens.prose: Two readings share $x = 1$: $(1, 10)$ and $(1, 20)$. There is also $(2, 30)$. Merge repeats by their mean, then interpolate at $x = 1.5$.
screens.question: What is $y$ at $x = 1.5$?

hints.text: What single $y$ stands for $x = 1$ after merging?
The mean of 10 and 20, which is 15.
Halfway from 15 to 30 is 22.5.

feedback.correct: 22.5: the repeats become 15, then halfway to 30.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Average the two readings at $x = 1$ first.

byKey.last: You kept the last reading, $(1, 20)$. That throws away the other one.
byKey.first: You kept the first reading, $(1, 10)$. That throws away the other one.

explain.text: The repeats merge to $(1, 15)$. Halfway to $(2, 30)$ is $15 + 7.5 = 22.5$.

screens.title: A missing value on uneven times
screens.prose: Readings at times 0, 1 and 4 are 100, missing and 112. Drop the missing value, then interpolate by time.
screens.question: What is the value at time 1?

hints.text: After dropping the gap, which two points remain?
Times 0 and 4. Time 1 is a quarter of the way across.

feedback.correct: 103: a quarter of the way from time 0 to time 4.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Interpolate by the time stamps, not by row position.

byKey.position: You filled by position, as if the three readings were evenly spaced. The stamps say time 1 is early.

explain.text: Time 1 is a quarter of the way from time 0 to time 4. So it gets a quarter of the rise. Filling by position gives 106, which is wrong here.

screens.title: interpolate() and the timestamps
screens.prose: A colleague says pandas `interpolate()` reads the timestamps in the index. The console shows the call and its result.
screens.question: What do you say?

options.text: By position; `method="index"` uses the stamps
It reads the index whenever the index holds dates
options.why: You assumed the index is used. The default `linear` method treats the values as evenly spaced.

options.text: It copies the value at the nearest timestamp
options.why: You mixed it up with `method="nearest"`. The default draws a straight line.

options.text: It fills with the mean of the whole series
options.why: You thought it averages everything. It uses the neighbours either side.

hints.text: Look at the result next to the index.
The index is 0, 1, 4 and the fill is 106, halfway between 100 and 112.
Halfway means by position. By time it would be 103.

feedback.correct: By position unless you ask for the index.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check the fill against the index.

byKey.dates: You trusted the index. Without `method="index"` or `"time"` the stamps are ignored.
byKey.near: You described `nearest`. The default draws a line between the neighbours.
byKey.mean: You described a global mean. The default uses only the two neighbours.

explain.text: The default treats the points as evenly spaced. For unevenly stamped data, say `method="index"` or interpolate by hand.

screens.title: Nothing left to interpolate
screens.prose: Every value in a column is missing. After you drop the gaps, no points remain.
screens.question: What should the interpolator do?

options.text: Raise an error or return NaN, and say which
Return 0, the safe default for a missing price
options.why: You invented a value. Zero is a price nobody quoted.

options.text: Return the last value it saw
options.why: There is no last value. You would pass off stale data.

options.text: Extrapolate from the first two rows
options.why: There are no rows to extrapolate from.

hints.text: Can any rule in the method produce a number?
The method needs at least one point to hold at the ends.
With none, say so; with one, return its value everywhere.

feedback.correct: Empty means no answer: raise or return NaN and say so.
feedback.generic: Not quite. With no points there is no honest number.

byKey.zero: You returned zero. A made-up number would flow into the next calculation.
byKey.last: You returned a value from nowhere. The input is empty.
byKey.line: You extrapolated from rows that do not exist.

explain.text: No points means no honest answer. One point means that point's value everywhere.

screens.title: Where the formula comes from
screens.prose: Two points $(x_0, y_0)$ and $(x_1, y_1)$ bracket $x$. The point $(x, y)$ is on the line between them.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. Leave out the step that does not belong.

lines.text: The three points are on one line, so the slopes match: $\dfrac{y - y_0}{x - x_0} = \dfrac{y_1 - y_0}{x_1 - x_0}$.
The fraction $\dfrac{x - x_0}{x_1 - x_0}$ is how far across the gap $x$ sits, so $y$ rises by that fraction of the rise.
Drop the division: $y = y_0 + (y_1 - y_0)(x - x_0)$.
lines.why: That drops the width of the gap. On $(0, 100)$ and $(10, 200)$ it gives 350 at 2.5, not 125.

hints.text: Start from equal slopes.
Clear the denominator on the left, then add $y_0$.
The fraction across the gap multiplies the rise.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Equal slopes, clear the denominator, add $y_0$.

byKey.x: You dropped the division by the gap width. The formula then depends on the units of $x$.
byKey.left-out: You left out a step the derivation needs.

explain.text: Equal slopes give the formula, and the fraction across the gap is the weight on the rise. At $x = 2.5$ that fraction is 0.25.

screens.title: Say it aloud
screens.prose: In one breath: sort, merge repeats, drop gaps, find the bracket, apply $y = y_0 + (y_1 - y_0)\dfrac{x - x_0}{x_1 - x_0}$, hold the ends.
screens.question: Which answer would you say?

options.text: I sort by x, average repeats, drop gaps, bisect for the bracket and hold the ends.
I fit one line through every point with polyfit and read the value off it, which is quick.
options.why: You fitted a global line. An interpolator passes through each point.

options.text: I fill each gap with the previous value, which is quick and safe.
options.why: You carried a value forward. That ignores the later point and makes steps.

options.text: I find the bracket and extend the last segment past the ends.
options.why: You extrapolated. Past the ends we hold the nearest value.

hints.text: The answer should name the order of the steps.
Look for sorting before the bracket and the ends held.
Only one answer names all of them.

feedback.correct: Sort, merge, drop, bracket, formula, hold the ends.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Choose the answer that names every step.

byKey.poly: You named a regression, not an interpolator.

explain.text: Say the steps in order. Sorting comes first, since bisection needs sorted $x$.

screens.title: Quotes with gaps
screens.prose: About ten minutes with the code. `ticks-gaps.csv` holds 312 quotes: 15 blank prices, and 12 seconds that appear twice. Clean it, then price any second two ways.
screens.question: Write `clean_ticks`, `price_at` and `price_at_np`.

widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests. They check the 286 clean rows and the columns. They check three interior prices and both ends from the bisection version (relative 1e-9). The same five come from numpy.interp, and a sweep checks the two agree.

hints.text: Drop blank prices first, then group by the second and average.
`bisect.bisect_right(ts, t)` gives the index just past the bracket's left point.
Return the first or last price outside the range, and `np.interp` does the same by itself.

feedback.correct: 286 clean times, and the two versions agree.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Drop blanks, average repeated seconds, sort, and hold the ends.

explain.text: Dropping 15 blanks leaves 297 quotes, and averaging repeated seconds merges 11 pairs, so 286 times remain. `numpy.interp` does the sort-free bracket search for you but needs sorted times.

screens.title: The follow-up
screens.prose: The interviewer asks: "Now do it for ten million rows."
screens.question: What do you answer?

options.text: Sort once, then vectorise every query with searchsorted
Keep the Python loop and run it on a bigger machine
options.why: You kept the loop. The cost is the interpreter, not the algorithm.

options.text: Fit a spline first, since splines are cheaper to evaluate
options.why: You swapped the method. A spline is not faster, and it changes the answers.

options.text: Sort the data again before each query to be safe
options.why: You repeated the sort. It costs $n \log n$ per query when once is enough.

hints.text: Where does the time go in the loop?
Each query pays Python overhead and, if you re-sort, a sort.
Sort once, then let numpy search all queries together.

feedback.correct: Sort once, then vectorise the search.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Remove the per-row Python work and the repeated sorting.

explain.text: Sort the points once. Then `np.searchsorted` or `np.interp` finds every bracket in a single vectorised call.

ideas: Sort the points, merge repeated x by their mean and drop missing values before you interpolate.
Find the bracketing pair by bisection, then add the fraction of the rise; past the ends hold the nearest value.
pandas fills by position unless you ask for the index, so uneven stamps need method="index".

formula.name: Linear interpolation
formula.note: For $x_0 \le x \le x_1$, the two points either side of $x$.

summary.trap: A default fill that looks right on evenly spaced data is wrong on uneven timestamps.

feedback.correct: 20: a quarter of the way up a rise of 40.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the fraction of the rise to 10.

byKey.unit: You added 1 to 10. The line rises 10 for each unit of $x$.

explain.text: A quarter of the way across gets a quarter of the rise of 40. That is 10, on top of 10.

quiz.question: What does the interpolator return at $x = 9$?

feedback.generic: Not quite. With one point, hold its value.

byKey.zero: You returned zero. The one point is the nearest value everywhere.

explain.text: One point is both ends of the data, so its value is held on both sides.

quiz.prose: Times 0, 3 and 4 hold 10, missing and 18. Interpolate by time.
quiz.question: What is the value at time 3?

feedback.correct: 16: three quarters of the way from 10 to 18.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Time 3 is three quarters of the way to time 4.

byKey.pos: You filled by position. The stamps are uneven, so halfway is wrong.

explain.text: Time 3 sits three quarters of the way across, so $10 + 0.75 \times 8 = 16$.

quiz.prose: A series has uneven timestamps in its index and one gap.
quiz.question: Which call fills the gap by time?

options.text: `s.interpolate(method="index")`
`s.interpolate()`
options.why: You used the default, which fills by position.

options.text: `s.ffill()`
options.why: You carried the last value forward. That draws no line.

options.text: `s.interpolate(method="nearest")`
options.why: You copied the nearest value. That draws no straight line.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask for the index method.

byKey.ffill: A forward fill draws no line.

explain.text: Only `method="index"` or `"time"` uses the stamps as the $x$ values.
